verses.text: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the offspring  of the Medes, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans,

in the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which Yahweh’s word  came to Jeremiah the prophet, for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years.
I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.
I prayed to Yahweh my God, and made confession, and said, Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments,
we have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even turning aside from your precepts and from your ordinances;
neither have we listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.

Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face, as it is today; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, who are near, and who are far off, through all the countries where you have driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against you.
Lord, to us belongs confusion of face, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you.
To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him;
neither have we obeyed Yahweh our God’s voice, to walk in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.

Yes, all Israel have transgressed your law, turning aside, that they should not obey your voice: therefore the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us; for we have sinned against him.

He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us, and against our judges who judged us, by bringing on us a great evil; for under the whole sky, such has not been done as has been done to Jerusalem.
As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil has come on us: yet have we not entreated the favor of Yahweh our God, that we should turn from our iniquities, and have discernment in your truth.
Therefore has Yahweh watched over the evil, and brought it on us; for Yahweh our God is righteous in all his works which he does, and we have not obeyed his voice.
Now, Lord our God, who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have gotten yourself renown, as it is today; we have sinned, we have done wickedly.

Lord, according to all your righteousness, let your anger and please let your wrath be turned away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain; because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a reproach to all who are around us.
Now therefore, our God, listen to the prayer of your servant, and to his petitions, and cause your face to shine on your sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord’s sake.

My God, turn your ear, and hear; open your eyes, and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name: for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.
Lord, hear; Lord, forgive; Lord, listen and do; don’t defer, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people are called by your name.
While I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God;
yes, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering.
He instructed me, and talked with me, and said, Daniel, I have now come to give you wisdom and understanding.
At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, and I have come to tell you; for you are greatly beloved: therefore consider the matter, and understand the vision.

Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy.

Know therefore and discern, that from the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem to the Anointed One,  the prince, shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: it shall be built again, with street and moat, even in troubled times.

After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One  shall be cut off, and shall have nothing: and the people of the prince who shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be with a flood, and even to the end shall be war; desolations are determined.

He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.

footnotes.content: Darius rules over Babylon now—a foreign king holding power in a land that isn't home. Daniel, aging, has learned to serve well under changing rulers, whether Nebuchadnezzar or now Darius, because his true loyalty has never been to any earthly throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years and grasps it in his bones—not as a distant prophecy but as *this moment*. The desolations are nearly complete. How often do we read Scripture and miss that we ourselves live in the **when**?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fasting, sackcloth, ashes—the body joins the soul in crying out to God. Daniel doesn't simply think about repentance; he embodies it. There's something honest about letting our posture teach our heart what mere words alone might skip over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Great and dreadful God"—Daniel begins not with his own need but with who God *is*. He names the covenant, the loving-kindness, the reward of obedience. Before we confess sin, sometimes we need to remember: this God is not small, and His promises are not rescinded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly." Notice Daniel uses "we"—not "they," not "our fathers alone." Real confession includes us. When we stand with the broken, God draws near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We have not listened to your servants the prophets." Israel had the word of God spoken through Jeremiah, through Isaiah, through others—yet turned away. How many of us have Scripture, pastors, wise counsel *right there*, and still harden our ears?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face." There's a gentleness in this confession—a clear-eyed sorrow that doesn't despair. God's righteousness is fixed; ours is shame. But shame named before Him is already the beginning of hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shame extends to "our kings, our princes, and our fathers." Daniel doesn't excuse the leaders or blame them alone—he holds the whole people, across generations, before God in one honest sorrow. Corporate repentance begins when one person refuses to let others hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness; for we have rebelled against him." Even in confession, Daniel anchors hope not in his sincerity but in God's mercies. Our confessions are weak; His forgiveness is infinite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We have not obeyed Yahweh our God's voice." The heart of it: not just sins of commission but disobedience—turning away from the voice that calls. And yet here, in exile, Daniel *is* listening. Repentance is the turn back toward that voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The curse and the oath written in the law of Moses...has been poured out on us." Daniel names the consequences written in Deuteronomy 28—exile was promised, and exile is come. God is just; Israel's sorrow is not meaningless suffering but the earned weight of turning away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Under the whole sky, such has not been done as has been done to Jerusalem." The devastation is complete—the temple burned, the people scattered, the land grieving. Sometimes we must name the full wound before we can receive healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All this evil has come on us: yet have we not entreated the favor of Yahweh our God." Here's the strange mercy: even in judgment, God leaves the door open. The people could *still* turn, *still* entreat His favor, *still* seek His truth in the ruins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh our God is righteous in all his works." Daniel doesn't argue with God's justice; he agrees with it. When we stop defending ourselves and simply say, "You are right to do what You've done," we open a space where God's mercy can work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand." Daniel holds up the exodus—God's greatest saving act—and lays it before Him: "You have done this before; the same God still stands." Memory of grace is the seedbed of intercession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let your anger and please let your wrath be turned away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain." Daniel asks not for what he deserves but for what matches God's own honor—the city that bears God's name, though defiled, is still God's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Cause your face to shine on your sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord's sake." Daniel prays for restoration not as a reward to the people but for God's own sake—because His own house lies broken, His own name is at stake. Sometimes we must appeal to God's glory, not our need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies' sake." Daniel strips away every claim, every bargain. We come empty-handed and still daring to pray—because we know He is merciful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Lord, hear; Lord, forgive; Lord, listen and do; don't defer, for your own sake, my God." The prayer crescendos into urgent pleading—*listen, forgive, do*—yet all for God's own glory and God's own name. This is intercession at its truest: we forget ourselves entirely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel prays for "the holy mountain of my God." Even now, in exile, Jerusalem remains *holy*—not because the city is pure, but because God claims it. Our prayers for places, for people, are most powerful when we pray for what God Himself holds dear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning." Gabriel appears before—at the birth of John the Baptist and at Mary's side—and here touches Daniel while he still prays. God's messenger comes precisely when and as God chooses, often while we are still seeking His face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have now come to give you wisdom and understanding." God answers Daniel's prayer not merely with comfort but with *revelation*. He names Daniel's great value: you are one through whom I will speak truth that echoes across centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out." The moment Daniel began to pray, God had already spoken. Our intercession is not us finally moving God's heart—it is us joining the work God has already begun in our behalf.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Seventy weeks are decreed...to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity." Readers today hear an echo here: Christ would come as the final Word, the end of exile and death, the reconciliation of God and mankind. In Jesus, all these promises converge. As of 2026-10, we see that ending written across the whole Gospel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "From the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem...shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks." Time is given measure; restoration is promised. In the longest night, a specific count of days offers hope—the exile will not last forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One shall be cut off." Sorrow and majesty twist together—the figure of hope will be cut off, will have nothing. Yet Daniel sees it, and in that seeing, God dignifies suffering that leads to redemption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week." A new covenant is promised, firm and binding. The old has been fulfilled, judged, and now God pours out a new covenant that will hold fast forever. That is the mercy toward which all exile points.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
